title: “A GOOD TREE CANNOT BEAR BAD FRUIT” — BUT WHAT IF JESUS WASN’T TALKING ABOUT THE FRUIT YOU THINK?
paragraphs: “A GOOD TREE CANNOT BEAR BAD FRUIT” — BUT WHAT IF JESUS WASN’T TALKING ABOUT THE FRUIT YOU THINK?
You can look alive in public while something is dying at the roots. Jesus was never impressed by decorated branches. He looked for the fruit that reveals who truly owns the heart.
There is something terrifying about a tree that still looks alive after its roots have begun to die.
The leaves may remain green for a while.
The branches may still move when the wind blows.
From a distance, nothing looks wrong.
People can walk past it and never suspect that beneath the soil, where nobody applauds and nobody photographs and nobody sees, death has already begun.
And maybe that is why the words of Jesus are so unsettling.
Because He wasn't merely talking about trees.
He was talking about us.
Jesus said:
“Οὐ γάρ ἐστιν δένδρον καλὸν ποιοῦν καρπὸν σαπρόν…”
Ou gar estin dendron kalon poioun karpon sapron…
“For no good tree bears bad fruit…”
The Greek word translated “fruit” is καρπός — karpos.
Fruit.
Produce.
What comes forth from something because of what that thing truly is.
And the word Jesus uses for bad fruit is σαπρός — sapros.
Rotten.
Corrupt.
Decayed.
Worthless.
Jesus is not describing a cosmetic problem.
He is describing something rotten coming from within.
And suddenly His words become much more uncomfortable.
Because Christianity can become cosmetic too.
You can learn Christian vocabulary.
You can post Bible verses.
You can know exactly when to say “Amen.”
You can raise your hands during worship while refusing to surrender what those hands keep reaching for in secret.
You can tell everyone that God is good while bitterness quietly poisons your heart.
You can defend biblical truth online and then destroy someone with your tongue at home.
You can know Christian theology and still refuse to forgive.
while something underneath the soil is starving.
Jesus said:
“Each tree is known by its own fruit.”
And then He went directly beneath the branches.
Into the heart.

“The good man brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart, and the evil man brings evil things out of the evil treasure of his heart. For out of the overflow of the heart, the mouth speaks.”
That is Luke 6:43–45.
Notice what Jesus does.
Tree.
Fruit.
Heart.
Mouth.
He connects them.
What eventually appears outside has been living somewhere inside.
That angry sentence you wish you could take back.
That jealousy you keep disguising as “discernment.”
That secret lust nobody knows about.
That appetite for attention.
That bitterness you rehearse when you're alone.
That habit of tearing people apart when they are not in the room.
That refusal to forgive while asking God every morning to forgive you.
That private compromise you have learned to manage instead of crucify.
Jesus is not merely interested in trimming the visible fruit.
He goes after the heart producing it.
And that changes the question.
The question is no longer simply:
“Do I sometimes do bad things?”

Every Christian still battles sin. Scripture does not teach that genuine believers become instantly sinless. Christians stumble. Christians need confession. Christians need correction. Christians need grace every single day.
The frightening question is different.
What is my life increasingly producing?
When sin appears, do I defend it or confess it?
When Christ confronts me, do I harden myself or surrender?
When nobody is watching, what do my desires reveal?
When someone wounds me, what begins growing inside me?
When God says no to something I desperately want, does Jesus remain enough?
When obedience costs me something...
do I still call Him Lord?
Because only moments after speaking about trees and fruit in Luke's account, Jesus asks a devastating question:
“Why do you call Me ‘Lord, Lord,’ but not do what I say?”
There it is.
Fruit is not Christian decoration.
Fruit is evidence.
Not evidence that earns salvation.
Evidence that something living has happened inside you.
A tree does not strain until it earns the right to become alive.
A living tree bears fruit because life is already flowing through it.
And this is where so many exhausted Christians have misunderstood Jesus.
They have heard “bear good fruit” and translated it:
“Try harder.”
“Look better.”
“Hide your failures.”
“Become impressive enough for God.”
“Make sure nobody discovers how badly you're struggling.”
But Jesus gives us another picture in John 15.
Not merely a tree.
A vine.
Branches.
And Himself.
“Μείνατε ἐν ἐμοί…”
Meinate en emoi.
“Remain in Me.”
“Abide in Me.”
Then Jesus explains that a branch cannot bear fruit from itself unless it remains in the vine.
And He says:
“ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἄμπελος…”
Egō eimi hē ampelos.
“I am the vine.”
Then comes the truth every exhausted believer needs to hear:
“χωρὶς ἐμοῦ οὐ δύνασθε ποιεῖν οὐδέν.”
Chōris emou ou dynasthe poiein ouden.
“Apart from Me you can do nothing.”
Maybe you have spent years trying to manufacture fruit while disconnected from the Vine.
Trying to manufacture patience.
Manufacture purity.
Manufacture joy.
Manufacture holiness.
Manufacture the appearance of spiritual health.
And eventually you became exhausted.
Because branches were never designed to manufacture life.
They receive it.
Jesus is not asking you to become your own Savior.
He is calling you to remain in the Savior you already desperately need.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus did not come merely to staple better fruit onto dying branches.
He came to make dead sinners alive.
He came for the hypocrite.
The addict.
The liar.
The sexually broken.
The bitter.
The proud.
The ashamed.
The religious performer.
The person who knows Scripture but has grown cold toward the God who spoke it.
The person secretly wondering whether they have ruined too much.
Maybe that person is you.
Maybe there are things in your life you would be terrified for anyone at church to discover.
Maybe you have learned how to smile while your soul is collapsing.
Maybe people call you strong because they have never heard what happens inside your mind at two in the morning.
Maybe your Bible has highlighted pages while your heart feels completely dark.
Maybe you have prayed:
“Jesus... why am I still like this?”
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say your sin is small.
The Gospel says the Savior is greater.
Jesus carried real guilt onto a real cross.
He was not crucified because humanity needed motivational improvement.
He was crucified because sin brings death and sinners needed reconciliation with God.
Christ died for sins.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose again.
Grace is not God pretending the rotten fruit doesn't smell.
Grace goes deeper.
Grace deals with the sinner.
Grace forgives.
Grace cleanses.
Grace reconciles.
Grace begins transformation.
Grace teaches us to stop hiding from the Gardener.
And perhaps that is the hardest part.
We want Jesus to remove consequences while leaving our favorite roots untouched.
We want peace without surrender.
Forgiveness without repentance.
Resurrection without crucifixion.
A crown without a cross.
We want Christ as Savior while negotiating whether He may actually be Lord.
But Jesus loves us too much to participate in our pretending.
In Matthew 7, the fruit warning becomes even sharper.
Jesus warns about false prophets who appear harmless but are inwardly dangerous. He says they will be recognized by their fruits.
Then He says:
“πᾶν δένδρον μὴ ποιοῦν καρπὸν καλὸν…”
Every tree not producing good fruit is cut down.
And only moments later Jesus says something that should silence every person tempted to confuse spiritual activity with knowing Christ:
Not everyone who says, “Lord, Lord,” will enter the kingdom of heaven.
Some will point to extraordinary things they did in His name.
Yet Jesus' response is terrifying:
“I never knew you.”
Think about that.
Religious activity was present.
Religious vocabulary was present.
Even astonishing works were claimed.
Yet something essential was missing.
This means the fruit Jesus seeks cannot simply mean looking impressive in religious spaces.
You can have activity without intimacy.
Visibility without holiness.
Ministry without surrender.
A platform without obedience.
Christian language without a transformed heart.
Jesus is looking deeper.
Paul later gives language to the kind of life the Holy Spirit produces:
“Ὁ δὲ καρπὸς τοῦ Πνεύματός…”
Ho de karpos tou Pneumatos…
“But the fruit of the Spirit…”
Love.
Joy.
Peace.
Patience.
Kindness.
Goodness.
Faithfulness.
Gentleness.
Self-control.
Notice something beautiful.
Paul says fruit.
Karpos.
The same basic Greek word for fruit.
The Spirit of God produces recognizable evidence in a life surrendered to God.
Not overnight perfection.
Not theatrical Christianity.
Not sinless performance.
Fruit.
And fruit grows.
Slowly sometimes.
Painfully sometimes.
Quietly sometimes.
A person who once exploded in rage begins learning gentleness.
Fruit.
Someone who lived for revenge begins praying for the person who wounded them.
Fruit.
Someone enslaved to secret sin falls again but no longer calls darkness home; they confess, seek help, repent, get back up, and run toward Christ instead of away from Him.
Fruit.
Someone who once needed everyone's approval discovers that being known by Jesus matters more than being applauded by people.
Fruit.
A husband apologizes without defending himself.
Fruit.
A wife chooses forgiveness without pretending the wound was acceptable.
Fruit.
A young believer deletes what keeps dragging them back into temptation.
Fruit.
A proud Christian finally says, “I was wrong.”
Fruit.
Someone nobody sees gives quietly because another person is hurting.
Fruit.
Someone who has been spiritually numb whispers after months of silence:
“Jesus... I want to come home.”
Fruit.
Do not despise small fruit.
A seedling is not a mature oak, but it is alive.
The question is not whether you have reached flawless Christian maturity.
The question is whether the life of Christ is producing something in you that wasn't there before.
And sometimes the most beautiful fruit begins with two words:
“I repent.”
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God refusing to abandon you inside what is destroying you.
It is turning.
Coming into the light.
Dropping the mask.
Stopping the negotiations.
Saying:
“Jesus, this is what I have become. This is what I have hidden. This is what I cannot repair. Have mercy on me.”
And discovering that the One you were afraid to approach already stretched His arms open on a cross.
That is Christianity.
Not rotten people learning how to spray perfume over decay.
Dead people being made alive in Christ.
Guilty people being forgiven.
Lost people being found.
Enemies being reconciled.
Captives being freed.
Sinners becoming sons and daughters by grace through faith.
Scandals becoming testimonies.
Ashes becoming places where mercy grows.
The cross means your worst chapter does not have to be your final chapter.
But grace is not permission to keep writing the same rebellion forever.
Grace takes the pen.
Grace changes the direction of the story.
Jesus rewrites everything.
So maybe tonight the question isn't:
“Do people think I'm a good Christian?”
Forget people for a moment.
Forget Facebook.
Forget church reputation.
Forget titles.
Forget how many verses you know.
Forget how convincing you sound when you pray.
Imagine yourself alone before Jesus Christ.
No audience.
No filters.
No reputation to protect.
Just you...
and Him.
What fruit has been growing?
What would your private conversations reveal?
What would your search history reveal?
What would the way you treat your family reveal?
What happens inside your heart when somebody else succeeds?
What comes out when you are tired, angry, disappointed, ignored, tempted, contradicted, or wounded?
What have you been feeding at the roots?
And here is the question beneath all the others:
Are you abiding in Jesus... or merely maintaining the appearance that you are?
Do not answer quickly.
Sit with it.
Because maybe this article didn't reach you so you could inspect everyone else's fruit.
Maybe Jesus is standing beside your tree.
Not to entertain your accusations against someone else.
But to ask about your roots.
And if something has been exposed, don't run.
Come into the light.
Confess it.
Repent.
Return.
There is mercy at the cross.
There is cleansing in Christ.
There is power in the Holy Spirit.
There is still hope for the branch that stops pretending it can live without the Vine.
You don't need to tell strangers every detail of your struggle. But sometimes bringing even a small confession into the light is the moment isolation begins losing its grip.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to preach at them.
Not because every sentence is comfortable.
Because someday you may need to remember again:
Fruit cannot be permanently manufactured by pretending.
We need the Vine.
We need Jesus.
Not as payment for God's favor.
Not as a way of purchasing blessing.
Not as a substitute for repentance, obedience, generosity to your local church, or any biblical responsibility.
If you have ever prayed, “Lord, use what I have for Your glory,” supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical expression of that desire.
Your sharing helps us keep reaching.
Your prayers help us keep standing.
And your support helps us build more resources for believers who are hungry to know Jesus more deeply.
Ultimately...
people need Jesus.
And before you leave, remember the tree.
People may admire the leaves.
They may applaud the branches.
They may never see the roots.
But Jesus does.
And the beautiful news of the Gospel is that when He exposes what is dying beneath the surface, He does not merely point at the decay.
He calls sinners to Himself.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He transforms.
He makes all things new.
So stop decorating what Jesus wants to resurrect.
Come back to the Vine.
Let Him reach the roots.
Let Him confront what is false.
Let Him heal what is wounded.
Let Him cut away what is killing you.
Let His Spirit grow what your flesh could never manufacture.
And one day, when somebody encounters your patience where anger used to live...
your forgiveness where bitterness once ruled...
your purity where lust once controlled you...
your humility where pride once demanded attention...
your generosity where selfishness once held tightly...
your courage where fear once imprisoned you...
your love where hatred once burned...
they may finally understand what Jesus meant.
The most convincing evidence that Jesus rewrote your story will not be the Christian label hanging from your branches—it will be the fruit growing where death used to be.
